subject: english
title: Phrasal verbs
description: The high-frequency ones — sort out, carry on, come up with — and where the object goes.

content.title: What makes them hard
content.body: A phrasal verb's meaning rarely follows from its parts: give up has nothing to do with giving. They have to be learned as single vocabulary items, in a sentence.

content.title: Separable or not
content.body: Many take the object either after the particle or between the two parts: turn off the light / turn the light off. A pronoun object must go in the middle: turn it off, never turn off it.

content.title: Good practice
content.body: In formal writing a single-word equivalent often reads better: resolve rather than sort out, postpone rather than put off. In speech the phrasal verb is the natural choice.

exercises.question: Vocabulary
exercises.explanation: She came up with a workaround. Three parts, and none of them can be dropped.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Can you ___ out the failing test before the demo?
exercises.explanation: sort something out means fix or resolve it. It is separable: sort it out, sort out the test.

exercises.question: Which sentence is correct?
exercises.explanation: With a separable phrasal verb, a pronoun object always sits between the verb and the particle.

exercises.question: Translate the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Musimy przełożyć wdrożenie na następny tydzień.

answers.text: We have to put the release off until next week.
We have to put away the release to next week.
We have to put the release down until next week.
We have to put off the release since next week.

exercises.explanation: put something off means postpone it, and until marks the new point in time.

exercises.question: "I ran my old manager into at the conference" is correct.
exercises.explanation: run into is inseparable, so the object follows the whole phrase: I ran into my old manager.

exercises.question: Why do phrasal verbs often get replaced in formal reports?

answers.text: They cannot be used in the past tense
Single-word Latin-based equivalents read as more formal
Phrasal verbs are grammatically incorrect in writing

exercises.explanation: find out → determine, put up with → tolerate, go up → increase. Both are correct English; the difference is register.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Ignore the warning and carry ___ with the deployment.
exercises.explanation: carry on means continue. carry out means perform or execute — carry out a test.

exercises.question: What does "I'll look into it" mean?

answers.text: I will look at it briefly and move on

exercises.explanation: look into means investigate. look after means take care of, look up means find in a reference.

exercises.question: Vocabulary
exercises.explanation: Near-universal in software English. The noun is a rollback, written as one word.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: It took us two days to figure ___ why the test only failed on CI.
exercises.explanation: figure something out means work it out or understand it after effort. It is separable: figure it out.

exercises.question: What does "We ended up rewriting the whole suite" mean?

answers.text: We finished rewriting it on time
That is what eventually happened, though it was not the plan

exercises.explanation: end up + -ing describes the unintended final outcome. The Polish equivalent is "skończyło się na tym, że...".

exercises.question: Translate the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Poprzyj to danymi, zanim wyślesz do klienta.

answers.text: Back it up with data before you send it to the client.
Back up it with data before you send to the client.
Backup it with data before sending to client.
Back it with data up before you send it.

exercises.explanation: back something up means support it with evidence, and a pronoun object goes in the middle. "Backup" as one word is the noun.

exercises.question: Three-part phrasal verbs such as "put up with" are inseparable.
exercises.explanation: The object always follows the whole phrase: I can't put up with it — never "put it up with".

exercises.question: What does "I haven't got around to it yet" convey?

answers.text: I have not found the time for it, though I intend to
I have refused to do it

exercises.explanation: A soft, common way of saying not yet done. The to is a preposition, so it takes a noun or -ing: got around to writing it.

exercises.question: Vocabulary
exercises.explanation: We narrowed it down to two suspects. Very common when describing debugging in English.
